lines: Night came to the forest, and one by one the little lights went out.
Little Bear Doudou lay in his bed.
He counted the last sheep, but he still could not sleep.
Wind slipped through the window, carrying the smell of green grass and lake water.
Then Doudou heard a very soft sound outside, like someone crying.
He put on his soft slippers and went to the door.
Moonlight lay on the ground like a silver path.
Doudou looked up and saw that the moon was missing a small corner, like a cookie with one bite taken out.
The moon sat beside a cloud and said softly,
“I lost a little piece of light. Without it, I cannot sleep tonight, and I cannot help light everyone’s dreams.”
“I will help you find it,” said Doudou.
The moon showed him a path made of moonlight. Doudou followed it into the forest.
The night forest was not frightening.
An owl kept watch in a tree.
A stream snored softly beside the stones.
Dewdrops sat quietly on the leaves.
Doudou walked more and more gently, as if he were afraid of waking someone.
In the grass, he met a little firefly who had lost its way.
The firefly said, “I saw a small piece of light fall into the hollow of the old oak tree.”
The hollow was dark and deep.
Doudou reached inside, and his heart beat fast.
He found something warm. It was not danger. It was a little piece of moonlight.
The moonlight rested in his paw and slowly turned into a soft moon candy.
When Doudou brought it close to his nose, it smelled like roasted chestnuts and blankets dried in the sun.
Doudou carried the moon candy back to the lake.
He held it up, and the moon leaned down and smiled.
It turned out that what the moon had lost was not just light.
It was the last dream of the night.
The moon became round again.
It poured its gentle light over Doudou’s bed and said,
“Thank you. Now I will give this little piece of light to you, to be your pillow.”
The moonlight wrapped around Doudou’s shoulders like a soft silk scarf.
Doudou went home and climbed under his blanket.
His pillow felt warm, as if a little moon were hidden inside.
The moon breathed slowly, in and out, like his mother patting his back.
Doudou closed his eyes.
He dreamed that he was sailing in a moon boat over a quiet forest.
Fireflies carried their lights ahead of him, and the wind pulled a cloud over him like a blanket.
The little rabbit, the squirrel, and the bird were all asleep, and a small piece of moonlight shone in their dreams too.
In the dream, the moon said to Doudou,
“Whatever you did not finish today can wait for tomorrow.
Whatever you did not say today can wait for a dream.
Just close your eyes, and give the rest to the night.”
Doudou listened and listened. His breathing became slow.
He felt as if he had turned into moonlight, falling gently on the treetops, on the lake, and into every dream that had already fallen asleep.
The next morning, Doudou woke up and found a little patch of silver light beside his pillow.
Outside, the forest was waking too.
A bird sang in the branches, and a squirrel stretched in its tree hollow.
Doudou hugged his pillow and smiled, because he knew it was the moon’s goodnight.
After that, Doudou sometimes still could not sleep. But he was no longer worried.
He would touch his pillow and remember the moon that night, and the kind thing he had done for a heart that could not sleep.
Then he would close his eyes and breathe slowly.
He would place his last little worry beside the pillow.
Goodnight, Doudou.
Goodnight, Moon.
Goodnight, forest.
Goodnight, little one.
